reading.rtitle: A Week Inside a Small Firm
paras: Marina Duarte runs a firm of seven lawyers in Curitiba. She specializes in commodity contracts: her clients buy and sell corn, soya and sugar, and they almost never meet the people on the other side of the deal. Marina does not go to court. She says a good week is a week in which nobody has to.

Her routine rarely changes. She arrives before eight and reads the overnight messages from Europe first, because Rotterdam is five hours ahead and the answer usually has to leave before lunch. She then reviews the contracts her associates prepared the day before. Rafael, the youngest associate, handles the smaller deals on his own; he sends her the difficult clauses and she reads every one of them.

The firm charges a fee for each contract and a second fee if a dispute starts. Marina explains this to every new client in the first meeting, because the client who understands the schedule of fees never argues about the invoice. She also explains what her firm does not do: it does not find buyers, it does not negotiate the price, and it does not sign anything for the client.

On Friday afternoons she stops. Nobody in the firm sends a contract for review after four o'clock on a Friday, and that rule is hers. She says the mistakes she has seen in twenty years almost all happened late on a Friday, in a hurry, on a document that somebody read once.
reading.source: A composite portrait of a Brazilian commodity practice, written for this lesson.

choices: To explain how to become a lawyer in Brazil.
To show what one commodity lawyer actually does in a normal week, and what she does not do.
To argue that firms should charge higher fees for contracts.

items.situation: Say what Marina does, in one sentence, using she.
tips: Watch the -s: she specialize is the mistake, she specializes is the form.

items.situation: Now say what she does NOT do. Two things from the text.
tips: She does not go to court.
Her firm does not negotiate the price. Note: after does not, the verb loses the -s.

items.situation: Ask a question about Rafael, using the third person.
tips: Does he handle the big deals too?
Not: Does he handles. The -s goes to does, never to both.

items.situation: The text says her routine rarely changes. Where does rarely go in the sentence?
tips: Before the verb: she rarely changes her routine.
With to be it goes after: she is rarely late.

listenings.text: People ask me what a commodity lawyer does all day, and the honest answer is that she reads. My associate reads the first version, I read the difficult clauses, and the client reads the summary we write in one page. Nobody in this office goes to court in a normal month. The work happens before the problem, not after it. A colleague of mine puts it very well. She says a contract is a machine for disagreeing politely, and if you build the machine properly, nobody ever has to use it. That is why we spend so long on the words. It also explains why we charge a second fee when a dispute starts. By then the machine has failed, and the work is a different kind of work.

Here is something that surprises people about the grain trade. The cargo often changes owner three or four times while the ship is still at sea. A trader in Geneva sells it to a buyer in Cairo, that buyer sells it again before the ship arrives, and every one of those sales has a contract behind it. Nobody sees the corn. What they see is a document. So the lawyer who works in this market never asks what the product looks like. He asks who owns it today, what the contract says about a late ship, and which country decides if the two sides disagree. That last question is the one that costs money when nobody answers it in advance.
